established_findings.statement: LLMs have been applied to network-configuration and NetOps tasks (intent-to-configuration, config generation, and prototypes for automated configuration agents).
limitations: Many sources are surveys or prototype demonstrations rather than large-scale production deployments.
Task scope and evaluation metrics vary across studies, limiting direct comparability.

established_findings.statement: Hallucination, overconfidence, and related failure modes in LLM outputs are widely documented; active research exists on detection, calibration, and mitigation methods (entropy-based detectors, ensemble/ensemble-judge, verification pipelines).
limitations: Most mitigation/detection results are reported on general-language or benchmark tasks; translation to NetOps-specific artifacts is not consistently evaluated.
Detection methods have varying true/false-positive trade-offs and may require task-specific tuning.

established_findings.statement: Generate–validate–repair (iterative generation with deterministic or heuristic validators and subsequent repairs) is a common workflow for improving LLM-produced artefacts; empirical work shows diminishing returns after a small number of repair iterations in related domains.
limitations: The diminishing-return finding is demonstrated across software-engineering tasks; direct measurement for NetOps configuration repair loops is limited.
Effectiveness depends strongly on validator quality and feedback design.

established_findings.statement: Tool-augmented LLM agents and orchestrated function-calling / external-tool use (specialized tools, validators, simulators, runtime frameworks) are proposed and shown to improve grounding and practical reliability in multi-step tasks.
limitations: Improvements are shown in prototype settings; integration complexity and latency trade-offs exist in operational environments.
The exact benefit depends on tool design, exposure strategy, and failure-handling mechanisms.

established_findings.statement: Human-in-the-loop safety and operator-approval patterns are described as practical mitigations for risky automated actions (pausing gray-zone operations for reviewer approval, blocking destructive actions), with applied implementations in non-network operational contexts.
limitations: Existing human-in-loop reports are from database, usability, and general-agent domains; direct NetOps operator studies are sparse.
Human approval workflows introduce latency and rely on appropriate reviewer tooling and training.

established_findings.statement: Community and research efforts have produced benchmarks, evaluation frameworks, and task suites for assessing LLMs on configuration and NetOps-like tasks (e.g., NetConfEval) and more general LLM-evaluation platforms.
limitations: Benchmarks differ in task definition, scope, and realism; many do not fully exercise operational safety properties like reachability, policy compliance, or staged rollout behavior.

unresolved_questions.statement: How reliably do LLM-generated network configurations satisfy deterministic operational properties at production scale (reachability, isolation, policy compliance) when assessed by formal network verifiers or simulators?
unresolved_questions.evidence_type: limited-evidence / gap identified from benchmarks and prototype reports
limitations: Existing work includes prototypes and benchmarks but lacks large-scale, verifier-driven empirical studies demonstrating end-to-end operational correctness.
Absence of evidence for large-scale production correctness should not be taken as evidence that LLMs cannot meet these properties under controlled tooling.

unresolved_questions.statement: What repair-loop iteration budgets and feedback designs are optimal for NetOps configuration repair (i.e., how many generate-validate-repair rounds are cost-effective for network configs)?
unresolved_questions.evidence_type: related-domain empirical finding; applicability to NetOps uncertain
limitations: Empirical result (diminishing returns around 3–4 iterations) comes from software-engineering tasks; NetOps artifacts may behave differently.
Network-operator cost, risk tolerance, and validator signal quality will affect optimal budgets.

unresolved_questions.statement: Which uncertainty- or calibration-based signals (e.g., semantic-entropy, log-likelihood variants, ensemble judges) best predict unsafe or incorrect network-change proposals in operational NetOps settings?
unresolved_questions.evidence_type: methodological literature with limited NetOps-specific validation
limitations: Proposed signals are validated on general benchmarks; domain transfer to structured network artifacts and deterministic validators is not yet established.
Calibration methods trade off between accuracy and coverage; operational thresholds remain to be determined.

candidate_gaps.statement: There is a need for reproducible, public datasets that pair realistic topologies, policies, and device-level configurations with verifier-oracle annotations (reachability, ACL semantics, isolation properties) to evaluate LLM-generated NetOps artifacts end-to-end.
candidate_gaps.evidence_type: benchmark and evaluation gap (inferred from existing benchmark scope)
limitations: NetConfEval and prototype studies exist but do not fully cover verifier-annotated, production-like corpora for deterministic property evaluation.
Creating such datasets has practical privacy and representativeness challenges (multivendor configs, proprietary policies).

candidate_gaps.statement: Network-specific studies of tool-execution hallucination (LLM agents making incorrect tool choices, invoking wrong APIs, or misinterpreting verifier feedback) are limited; existing taxonomies are general and not NetOps-tailored.
candidate_gaps.evidence_type: taxonomy papers and tool-framework reports indicating an application gap
limitations: Taxonomies and mitigation techniques exist for tool agents generally, but targeted NetOps red-team or failure-mode studies are sparse.
Network tooling often has idiosyncratic schemas and side effects that may amplify tool-execution hallucinations.

candidate_gaps.statement: Comparative empirical evaluations contrasting autonomous LLM-agent NetOps workflows with human-operator processes (efficiency, error modes, time-to-repair, safety) are scarce.
candidate_gaps.evidence_type: usability / HITL literature showing need for domain-specific comparative studies
limitations: Usability studies and HITL frameworks exist in general agent domains; direct controlled comparisons in NetOps contexts have limited published evidence.
Operator heterogeneity and organizational processes complicate generalization.

candidate_gaps.statement: Operational decision rules for gating LLM-suggested network changes (combining verifier outputs, confidence/calibration signals, and human review policies) lack empirically validated standards.
limitations: Individual components (uncertainty estimation, HITL gates, repair loops) are proposed; integrated, empirically validated gating policies for NetOps are not yet standardized.
Operational constraints (latency, staffing) will affect feasible policy design.

excluded_claims: LLMs are currently demonstrated to be production-ready for fully autonomous NetOps without human oversight.
Any single paper in the supplied records proves that LLMs reliably produce verifier-correct configurations at scale.
This set of records contains evidence that LLM-generated NetOps agents eliminate the need for deterministic network verifiers.
